course_name: EKYC User Journey – Complete Step-by-Step Onboarding Guide (1)
course_description: A complete step-by-step guide of the EKYC (Electronic Know Your Customer) onboarding process enabling new users to digitally open a trading and demat account with PhillipCapital without any physical paperwork.
course_objective: A way for RMs to help leads finish process faster
target_audience: New joiners (0–1 yr), Existing RMs (1–3 yr), AVP / Senior RM (3+ yr)

modules.title: Mobile & Email Verification
modules.text:
Step 1 – Mobile Number Registration
● Enter a valid 10-digit Indian mobile number (country code +91 pre-filled)
● Accept the mandatory Terms & Conditions checkbox
● Click Send OTP to receive a 6-digit OTP via SMS
● Existing users with incomplete applications can re-enter their mobile number to resume
● OTP is time-sensitive — if not entered within the validity period, use Resend OTP
Step 2 – Confirm Mobile OTP
● Mobile number is pre-filled and non-editable; a Change link is available to go back
● Enter the 6-digit OTP received via SMS
● A countdown timer is displayed; once expired, Resend OTP link appears (reset timer: 2
minutes)
● Click Continue to verify the OTP and proceed to email verification
Step 3 – Email ID Verification
● Enter a valid, accessible personal or professional email address
● Click Send OTP to receive a verification OTP on the entered email
● This email will be the primary email for all account-related communications from
PhillipCapital
Step 4 – Email OTP Verification
● Email ID is pre-filled with a Change link available
● Enter the 6-digit OTP sent to the email address
● A 2-minute countdown resend timer is shown
● Click Continue to validate and proceed to PAN & KRA verification
● Check Spam/Junk folder if the OTP email is not visible in Inbox

modules.title: PAN & Aadhaar KYC Verification
modules.text:
Step 5 – PAN Card & KRA Verification
● Mandatory fields: First Name, Last Name, PAN Number (10-character alphanumeric),
Date of Birth — all must match PAN card exactly
● Middle Name and Referral Code are optional
● Check the mandatory confirmation checkbox to authorize the KRA lookup
● Click Continue to trigger a real-time check against the KRA database
● If existing KYC records are found, details are pre-filled automatically in subsequent steps
● Any mismatch in name or date of birth with Income Tax records will result in verification
failure
Step 6 – Aadhaar KYC via Digi Locker
● PhillipCapital fetches a masked PDF copy of the Aadhaar card (name, gender, DoB,
address, photo) from Digi Locker — full Aadhaar number is NOT exposed
● Aadhaar and PAN must both belong to the same applicant
● Click Continue to Digi Locker and log in using Aadhaar-linked mobile OTP or Digi Locker
credentials
● Authorize PhillipCapital to access your Aadhaar data
● If Aadhaar and PAN belong to different persons, the application will be rejected

modules.title: Personal & Additional Details
modules.text:
Step 7 – Personal Details (Profile)
● Applicant Name is pre-filled from PAN/KRA — non-editable
● Select Title, Gender, and Marital Status from dropdowns
● Enter Father's name (single applicants) or Spouse's name (married applicants) —
mandatory
● Enter Mother's maiden name — mandatory
● Correspondence Address is pre-filled from Aadhaar/KRA and treated as the permanent
address
● Address changes must be done offline or post account opening at a PhillipCapital branch
Step 8 – Additional Details
● Professional details: Occupation Type, Work Profile, Company/Business Name, Address
of Occupation, Years of Experience, Source of Income
● Trading details: Who will place orders (Self or Authorized Person), Income Range, Net
Worth, Educational Qualification, Trading/Investment Experience, Running Account
Settlement preference (Monthly/Quarterly)
● Other: Whether dealing with any other broker; Electronic Contract Note preference (Yes
recommended)
● Mandatory compliance declarations:
○ PEP (Politically Exposed Person) — 3 declarations required
○ FATCA — Are you a U.S.
Person?
(Yes triggers additional documentation)
○ CRS — Are you a taxpayer outside India?
(Yes may require CRS documentation)
● Incorrect disclosures can lead to account suspension or legal complications
Step 9 – Contact Details
● Primary mobile number and email ID are pre-filled and non-editable (verified in Steps
1–4)
● Optionally add an alternate mobile number and/or alternate email address
● Click Continue to proceed to Nominee Details
Step 10 – Nominee Details
● Can add up to 3 nominees or choose to skip (nominees can be added post account
activation)
● Nominee fields: Name, Share % (all nominees must total 100%), Relationship, Date of
Birth, Address, Mobile, Email, Pin Code
● City and State auto-fill from pin code
● If nominee is a minor (under 18), Guardian Name is compulsory
● Identity proof for nominees and guardians must be uploaded in the Document Upload
step

modules.title: Bank Details & Account Setup
modules.text:
Step 12 – Bank Details
● Enter the 11-character IFSC code; click Find Bank Details to auto-fill Bank Name,
Address, and MICR Code
● Enter bank account number and re-enter for confirmation
● Click Verify Bank Details to trigger penny-drop verification (a small token amount
credited to confirm the account)
● Bank account must be in the applicant's own name — joint accounts or accounts in
another person's name are not accepted
● Token amount is not refunded but is negligible

modules.title: Payment, Brokerage, & Document Upload
modules.text:
Step 13 – Segment Selection & Account Opening Fee
● Segments to select:
○ Equity: Stocks, MF, ETFs — sub-exchanges: NSE, BSE, Mutual Funds, SLBs
○ Futures & Options: Derivatives — sub-exchanges: NFO, BFO, CDS
○ Commodity: sub-exchanges: NSE, BSE, NCDEX, MCX
● Additional options: Regular DEMAT Account (recommended for active traders), DDPI
(enables seamless debit of securities)
● Choose depository: NSDL or CDSL
● Fee is dynamically calculated based on segments selected; click Pay & Continue to
proceed to Razorpay
● Segments can be activated later but the opening fee applies separately for each
Step 14 – Payment Gateway (Razorpay)
● UPI: Scan QR code or enter UPI ID (2-minute QR validity timer)
● Cards: Debit or Credit — Visa, Mastercard, RuPay supported
● Netbanking: Redirects to the bank's login page
● Wallet: Amazon Pay, Freecharge, Mobikwik
● Available offers and price summary displayed before payment
● Payment is non-refundable once processed — keep payment confirmation for records
Step 15 – Brokerage Plan Selection
● Trade Professional Plan: Rs.
20/order flat brokerage across all segments — for
self-directed traders; Rs.
20 per order for Intraday and Delivery on Equities, Futures, and
Options
● Trade Support Plan: Percentage-based — Equities Intraday 0.10%, Delivery 0.50%;
Futures 0.05%; Options Rs.
30/lot; includes VAR+ELM Margin, collateral-based buying,
no restriction on intraday square-off, dedicated RM support; restriction on T2T/Z group
stocks
● Plan can be changed later by contacting the RM or PhillipCapital customer support
Step 16 – Upload Documents
● PAN Card photo/scan — mandatory (PDF/JPG/PNG, max 3 MB)
● Bank Proof — mandatory: cancelled cheque, passbook front page, or bank statement
showing account number, IFSC, and account holder name (PDF/JPG/PNG, max 3 MB)
● Signature Copy — mandatory: clear image on plain white background, preferably with
black or blue pen (JPG/PNG, max 3 MB)
● Documents must be clear, readable, and free from blur or shadows — blurry documents
result in rejection
● If nominees were added, identity proof for nominees (and guardians if minor) must also
be uploaded

modules.title: Final Verification & Application Completion
modules.text:
Step 17 & 18 – Selfie / IPV Capture
● SEBI requires a live photo/video verification (IPV) to confirm the applicant is physically
present
● Requirements: no sunglasses, no caps or hats, no face coverings; take in a well-lit
environment
● Photo must be a live selfie — photographing a printed or on-screen image is not allowed
● Grant Camera and Location access when prompted by the browser
● Align face within the circular guide and tap the capture button
● If Multiple Face Found error appears — ensure only your face is visible and retry
● Device must have a front-facing camera; Camera and Location access is mandatory
Step 19 & 20 – Annexure Review & Application PDF
● Review all regulatory annexure documents before signing:
○ Rights & Obligation (Trading and DP)
○ Risk Disclosure
○ Policies and Procedures
○ Do's and Don'ts for Trading on Exchange
○ PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002) disclosure
○ Other Terms and Conditions
○ MITC (Most Important Terms and Conditions)
● Check the mandatory confirmation checkbox declaring all documents have been read
● Click Review Ekyc Application to open the complete 64-page Client Registration Form
PDF
● Scroll through and verify all details are correctly reflected — this is the last opportunity to
correct anything before signing
● Once signed, changes require a formal request to PhillipCapital
Step 21 – eSign with Aadhaar OTP
● Click eSign With Aadhaar to initiate the Aadhaar eSign process
● An OTP is sent to the Aadhaar-linked mobile number — this may be different from the
mobile registered in Step 1
● Enter the OTP to complete the legally binding digital signature
● Ensure you have access to your Aadhaar-linked mobile number before proceeding
Step 22 – Application Completion
● Confirmation screen: "Your Application Process to E-KYC e-sign verification has been
Completed"
● Account activation normally takes 24–48 hours after successful eSign
● Download and save the signed application PDF using Esign Download & Print
● Check registered email and mobile for account activation confirmation from PhillipCapital
● Contact your respective RM for any support
● Once activated, download the PhillipCapital trading platform or log in at the web portal
Regulatory Compliance & Data Privacy
● Process complies with SEBI circulars on digital onboarding and eSign regulations
● PAN and Aadhaar linkage mandatory as per Income Tax Act provisions
● IPV via live selfie is mandatory as per SEBI/exchange guidelines
● Aadhaar-based eSign is legally valid under the Information Technology Act, 2000
● All personal data handled in accordance with applicable Indian data protection laws
● Aadhaar data fetched via Digi Locker does NOT include the full Aadhaar number
● Bank account verification done via penny-drop — internet banking credentials are never
collected

In traditional computer programming, a human writes strict rules.
For example: "If an email
contains the word 'Winner', move it to the Spam folder."
Machine Learning (ML) changes this.
Instead of writing rules, we give the computer data and let
it figure out the rules by itself.
● The Analogy: Imagine teaching a child to recognize a dog.
You don’t give them a manual
of rules about ear size and tail length.
You show them 50 dogs and say, "This is a dog."
Eventually, the child's brain recognizes the pattern of a dog.
Machine Learning does the
exact same thing with data.
3.
The Three Ways AI Learns
Scientists train AI using three primary methods.
A.
Supervised Learning (Learning with a Teacher)
This is the most common type of AI training.
We give the AI data where the answer is already
provided.
These answers are called labels.
● Example: We show the AI 10,000 photos of houses, and each photo is labeled with its
actual selling price.
The AI studies the photos and learns how size, location, and
bedrooms affect the price.
Now, when you show it a new photo of a house, it can guess
the price accurately.
B.
Unsupervised Learning (Learning Alone)
Here, we give the AI data with no labels and no answers.
We ask the AI to find hidden patterns
on its own.
● Example: A streaming service gives an AI a list of millions of users and the songs they
like.
The AI automatically groups users with similar tastes together into "clusters,"
allowing the system to recommend new music.
C.
Reinforcement Learning (Trial and Error)
This method uses a system of rewards and penalties.
The AI is placed in an environment and
learns by trying things out.
● Example: To teach an AI to play a video game, it gets "points" (rewards) for staying alive
and penalties for crashing.
After playing millions of times, it learns the perfect strategy to
win.
4.
The Brain: Deep Learning & Neural Networks
You have likely heard the term Deep Learning.
This is just a highly advanced type of Machine
Learning.
Deep Learning uses Artificial Neural Networks, which are software systems loosely inspired by
the human brain.
● Think of a neural network as a giant assembly line of digital filters.
● When you upload a photo of a face, the first layer of the network detects basic lines and
edges.
● The next layer combines those lines to recognize shapes like eyes and noses.
● The final layer puts it all together to say, "That is a human face."
Deep Learning is the technology behind self-driving cars, facial recognition, and smart tools like
ChatGPT.
[IMAGE: img_23]
[IMAGE: img_24]

modules.title: Module 3: Generative AI and the Future of Work
modules.text:
Module 3: Generative AI and the Future of Work
We learned how Machine Learning looks at data to recognize patterns.
Now, we are exploring
Generative AI—the technology that uses those patterns to create brand new content.
Instead of just analyzing data, Generative AI creates things: text, images, music, and even
computer code.
1.
What is Generative AI?
Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that generates new content based on user
prompts.
It is powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).
These models have read billions of pages of
human text from books, articles, and websites.
Because they have seen so much human
language, they understand how words fit together.
● The Predictor Analogy: Think of an LLM as a highly advanced version of the
autocomplete feature on your smartphone.
When you type a prompt, the AI predicts the
next most logical word, sentence, and paragraph based on all the text it has ever read.
2.
Text vs.
Image Generators
Generative AI primarily fits into two popular categories:
A.
Text Generators (The Writers)
Tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude can write, summarize, and brainstorm.
● How they help: They can draft emails, translate languages, write essays, code software,
or summarize a 50-page report into three bullet points.
B.
Image Generators (The Artists)
Tools like Midjourney, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion create visuals from scratch.
● How they help: Instead of searching stock photo websites, a designer can type "a
cinematic photo of an astronaut riding a horse on Mars," and the AI will generate that
exact image in seconds.
3.
The Art of the Prompt
The quality of AI output depends entirely on your instruction.
This instruction is called a prompt.
The emerging skill of writing great prompts is called Prompt Engineering.
To get the best results from a text AI, use the C-T-C Framework:
● Context: Tell the AI who it is.
(e.g., "You are a professional social media manager.")
● Task: Clearly state what you need.
(e.g., "Write three Instagram captions about our new
eco-friendly water bottle.")
● Constraints: Give it boundaries.
(e.g., "Keep each caption under 50 words and use an
energetic tone.")
4.
The Critical Catch: Hallucinations
Generative AI is brilliant, but it has a major flaw: Hallucinations.
Because these systems predict words based on mathematical patterns rather than looking up
verified facts, they can confidently make things up.
● An AI might invent a fake historical date, quote a law that does not exist, or generate a
broken math formula.
● The Golden Rule of Generative AI: Always fact-check the output.
Treat the AI like a
brilliant but slightly careless intern.
5.
AI and the Future of Work
AI is not taking over the world, but it is changing how we work.
● The Shift: AI is shifting humans from creators to editors.
Instead of spending three hours
writing a generic business proposal from scratch, a human uses AI to draft it in ten
seconds, then spends twenty minutes polishing, refining, and humanizing it.
● The Reality: AI likely won't replace your job, but a professional who knows how to use AI
might replace someone who doesn't.
[IMAGE: img_29]
[IMAGE: img_30]

modules.title: Module 4: AI in the Real World
modules.text:
Module 4: AI in the Real World
Now that you know what AI is and how it generates content, let’s look at how it impacts our
everyday lives.
AI is no longer a technology of the future; it is actively running behind the scenes
of our favorite apps, industries, and services.
1.
AI in Entertainment and Media
You likely interact with AI daily without even realizing it through recommendation systems.
● Streaming Services: Platforms like Netflix, Spotify, and YouTube use unsupervised
machine learning.
They track your watch history, skip rates, and search habits to predict
exactly what show or song will keep you hooked.
● Social Media: Feeds on Instagram, TikTok, and X use AI to analyze how many seconds
you linger on a post.
The algorithm then automatically curates a personalized timeline
tailored to your psychology.
2.
AI in Healthcare
AI is revolutionizing medicine by assisting doctors and saving lives.
● Disease Detection: Deep learning algorithms can scan thousands of X-rays, MRIs, and
CT scans.
They often detect tiny tumors or fractures faster and more accurately than
human eyes.
● Drug Discovery: Developing a new medicine usually takes scientists over a decade.
AI
can simulate millions of chemical combinations in seconds, shortening the drug
discovery timeline to just a few months.
3.
AI in Finance and Shopping
Money and commerce rely heavily on automated algorithms.
● Fraud Prevention: When you swipe your credit card, an AI instantly checks if the
transaction matches your usual spending habits.
If you live in New York and your card is
suddenly swiped in Paris, the AI flags it as fraud immediately.
● E-Commerce: Websites like Amazon use AI to forecast inventory demands and change
prices in real-time based on supply, demand, and your personal browsing history.
4.
AI in Transport and Travel
Moving from point A to point B is increasingly managed by smart software.
● Navigation Apps: Google Maps and Apple Maps use AI to analyze historical traffic
patterns, live user speeds, and construction data to calculate your fastest route.
● Autopilot & Autonomous Driving: Commercial airplanes fly on AI autopilot for most of
their journey.
Meanwhile, self-driving cars use cameras and radar to process road
environments instantly.
[IMAGE: img_35]

modules.title: Module 5: The Darkside of AI (Ethics, Bias, Safety)
modules.text:
Module 5: The Darkside of AI (Ethics, Bias, Safety)
While AI offers incredible benefits, it also brings massive challenges.
Because AI is built by
humans and trained on human data, it inherits our flaws, mistakes, and prejudices.
1.
The Problem with Algorithmic Bias
Remember the golden rule from Module 2: Garbage in, garbage out.
If an AI is trained on
biased data, its decisions will be biased.
● Real-World Example: A major tech company built an AI hiring tool to sort through job
resumes.
Because the historical data showed that most past software engineers were
men, the AI mistakenly learned that men were preferable candidates and actively
downgraded resumes containing the word "women's" (e.g., "women's chess club").
2.
Deepfakes and Misinformation
Generative AI makes it incredibly easy to alter reality.
● Deepfakes: These are AI-generated videos, images, or audio clips that look and sound
exactly like real people saying or doing things they never did.
● The Danger: Deepfakes can be used to scam individuals, manipulate political elections,
or ruin reputations by spreading highly convincing fake news.
3.
Copyright and Intellectual Property
Where do AI models get their knowledge?
They scrape billions of images and articles from the
open internet.
● The Controversy: Many human artists, authors, and journalists are suing AI companies.
They argue that AI models are using their copyrighted work without permission,
payment, or credit to generate competing content.
4.
Workforce Displacement
AI will automate many repetitive tasks currently done by humans.
● The Shift: Jobs involving basic data entry, simple customer service, basic copywriting,
and routine coding are experiencing major shifts.
While AI creates new tech jobs, it
requires workers to quickly upskill to avoid being left behind.
[IMAGE: img_38]

modules.title: Module 6: Master the Machine (Prompting basics)
modules.text:
Module 6: Master the Machine (Prompting basics)
To close out this course, you will learn the most critical practical skill for the AI era: Prompt
Engineering.
This section teaches you exactly how to talk to an AI to get perfect results on your
very first try.
1.
Avoid the "Google Search" Mistake
Most beginners treat AI like a search engine, typing short keywords like: "marketing plan for
coffee shop."
● The Result: The AI gives a generic, boring response because it has no context.
● The Fix: Treat the AI like a highly capable human assistant.
Give it specific rules,
background information, and a clear goal.
2.
The Golden Prompt Blueprint
Whenever you want an AI to write, brainstorm, or analyze, use this four-part formula:
\(\text{Role}+\text{Context}+\text{Task}+\text{Format}\)
● Role: Tell the AI who it is.
(e.g., "Act as a fitness coach.")
● Context: Give it the background story.
(e.g., "I am a busy office worker who wants to lose
5kg, but I only have 20 minutes a day to exercise.")
● Task: Clearly state what you need done.
(e.g., "Create a 5-day home workout plan.")
● Format: Tell it how to present the answer.
(e.g., "Put this in a clean markdown table with
columns for exercise name, reps, and rest time.")
3.
Three Pro-Tips for Better AI Results
● Give Examples (Few-Shot Prompting): If you want the AI to write a specific style of
newsletter, paste two of your past newsletters first and say, "Learn my style from these
examples, then write a new post about..."
● Iterate and Refine: Never settle for the first answer.
If the response is too long, tell the AI:
"Make it 30% shorter and more casual."
● Ask the AI to Ask You Questions: If you aren't sure what details to provide, type: "I want
to launch a website.
Ask me 5 questions one by one to gather the info you need to build
a strategy."

modules.title: Client Meeting Techniques & Relationship Management
modules.text:
Client Meetings — Approach, Pitch & Follow-up
● Pre-meeting preparation:
○ Research the client via MCA21, ZaubaCorp, or LinkedIn
○ Review existing portfolio or lead history in PhillipX
○ Prepare 2–3 relevant product ideas — never go empty-handed
○ Carry visiting card, brochures, and a note-taking tool
● During the meeting — 70/30 rule (70% listening, 30% talking):
○ Open with context: understand what the client wants to achieve
○ Ask needs discovery questions: investment goals, time horizon, risk appetite,
current investments
○ Never pitch in the first meeting unless the client specifically asks
○ Build rapport before product — ask about their business/profession first
○ End with a clear next step: confirm a follow-up date for a proposal
● What NOT to do: walk in and immediately pitch, make price predictions or return
guarantees, lie about product performance, take phone orders verbally without logging
● Follow-up and relationship building:
○ Call every client at least once per week — to connect, not to pitch
○ Read market news daily — be able to have an informed 5-minute conversation
○ Speak in themes, not tips: e.g., "IT sector has been volatile this quarter"
○ Acknowledge important dates: business anniversaries, major life events
○ Tell clients about compounding — time in the market is the message
SWOT & Personal Revenue Strategy
● Strengths to identify: client servicing, communication, network, product depth
● Weaknesses to acknowledge: market knowledge gaps, activity discipline, follow-up
consistency, compliance awareness
● Two strategies to pick from (commit to one):
○ Client-wise: choose one segment (Retail / Affluent / HNI) and go deep
○ Product-wise: choose 2–3 products you know best, find the right client type
● 4 patterns every RM must avoid:
○ Stop Acquiring — relying on the existing book; new blood is always needed
○ Cave Under Pressure — violating guidelines when targets are missed; always
ends worse
○ Stop Learning — not keeping up with markets and regulatory changes; credibility
falls fast
○ Organisational Dishonesty — misreporting meetings, faking activities; discipline
builds long careers
Dormant Account Revival
● Four reasons accounts go dormant:
○ Age/Life stage — reposition to fixed income, bonds, SLB
○ Loss — acknowledge loss first, rebuild trust, do not pitch immediately
○ Goal not achieved — review new goals, fresh conversation
○ Lost relationship — personal call from new RM, no pitch in first 2 calls
● Revival process:
○ Pull account history from PhillipX: last transaction, last MOM, last contact
○ Identify the reason for dormancy
○ Close the gap — address why it went dormant before pitching anything
○ Propose a fresh start: understand where the client is today
○ Do NOT lead with product in the first revival call
● Post-account-opening non-negotiables:
○ Flag any unusually large trade to the dealing desk
○ All trades must be recorded — no verbal or informal confirmations
○ No orders over the phone — all orders through the approved system
○ Initiate all communication in English
○ Answer dealing room phone within one ring, always with "PhillipCapital"

modules.title: Core AI Concepts and Technologies
modules.text:
Some Complex Topics:
If you are interested to learn more about AI you must learn the following 5 concepts:
Neural Networks:
- A system of connected nodes arranged in layers that process data
- Data goes in one end, flows through layers, and a result comes out
- Training adjusts internal weights each time the model gets something wrong
- After enough training it handles examples it has never seen before
- All modern AI — LLMs, image generators, voice models — are neural networks
Frontier Models vs Open source models:
- Frontier models are the most powerful proprietary models (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini)
- Accessed via API and charged per use; weights are kept private by the company
- Open source models have publicly released weights (Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
The models
used by the PhillipCapital chgatbot is open source.
- Open source gives full control and can be cheaper at scale but needs own infrastructure
- Choice depends on capability needed, control required, and budget
[IMAGE: img_21]
Embedding Model:
- Converts text (or images, audio) into a list of numbers called a vector
- Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together in numerical space
- "Dog" and "puppy" will be close; "dog" and "skyscraper" will be far apart
- Turns unstructured language into something computers can compare mathematically
- Foundation of search, recommendations, and any "find similar content" feature
[IMAGE: img_25]
Cosine Similarity:
- Measures how similar two vectors are by calculating the angle between them
- Score of 1.0 = identical meaning; -1.0 = opposite; 0 = unrelated
- Uses angle not straight-line distance — unaffected by length of text
- Used in vector search to find the most relevant content for a query
[IMAGE: img_28]
Vector database
- A database built to store embeddings and search through them at speed
- Returns the closest matching vectors to a query — called nearest neighbour search
- Unlike SQL, finds fuzzy meaning-based matches rather than exact keyword matches
- Popular options: Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma, pgvector
- The backbone of any RAG system connecting AI to your private documents
These five concepts form the foundation of everything in modern AI.
A neural network is the
engine.
An embedding model is how meaning gets turned into numbers.
Cosine similarity is
how those numbers get compared.
A vector database is where they get stored and searched.
And understanding the difference between frontier and open source models tells you which
engine to pick for any job.
Once these click, the intermediate concepts — RAG, agents, transformers, orchestration —
become much easier to understand because they are all just these five ideas combined in
different ways.
That is what the next module covers.

[IMAGE: img_32]

modules.title: Module 1: What is Artificial Intelligence?
modules.text:
Module 1: What is Artificial Intelligence?
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human cognitive processes by machines,
particularly computer systems.
These processes include learning, reasoning, problem-solving,
perception, and decision-making.
Instead of being explicitly programmed for every specific
scenario, AI systems use data and algorithms to continuously improve their accuracy and
autonomy.
To understand AI at a glance, it is helpful to look at its core components, types, and real-world
applications:
AI is an umbrella term that relies on several foundational technologies to function:
● Machine Learning (ML): Systems learn from historical data to make predictions or
decisions without being explicitly programmed.
● Deep Learning: A subset of ML that uses multi-layered artificial neural networks to
simulate the complex decision-making of the human brain.
● Natural Language Processing (NLP): Enables computers to understand, interpret, and
generate human language, powering chatbots and virtual assistants.
Types of AI:
AI is generally classified by its capabilities and complexity:
● Artificial Narrow Intelligence (ANI / Weak AI): AI designed to perform specific, narrow
tasks (e.g., chess engines, recommendation systems, or autonomous driving).
This is
the only type of AI that exists today.
● Artificial General Intelligence (AGI / Strong AI): A theoretical state where machines
possess human-level cognitive abilities, allowing them to learn and reason across a wide
variety of domains.
This remains strictly in the realm of theory and research.
● Generative AI: Systems capable of producing original text, images, audio, or video in
response to user prompts, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).
Everyday Examples
AI underpins many modern digital experiences, including:
● Digital Assistants: Systems like Alexa, Siri, or Google Gemini.
● Search Engines: Advanced web search algorithms that parse and rank information
instantly.
● Content Creation: Tools that generate articles, draft emails, or create digital art.

modules.title: Module 2: How AI Thinks (Data & Machine Learning)
modules.text:
Module 2: How AI Thinks(Data & Machine Learning)
We learned what Artificial Intelligence is.
Now, we are going to pull back the curtain and
look at how it actually works.
Many people think AI is magic, but it is actually just math, patterns, and a lot of
information.
1.
The Fuel of AI: What is Data?
Just like a car needs fuel to run, an AI needs data to think.
AI cannot learn anything without
information.
Data is simply a collection of facts, numbers, or items.
There are two main types of data that AI uses:
● Structured Data: Highly organized information.
Think of an Excel spreadsheet with neat
rows of numbers, dates, and names.
● Unstructured Data: Messy, everyday information.
This includes photos, emails, youtube
videos, and voice recordings
The Golden Rule of AI: Garbage in, garbage out.
If you feed an AI bad, incorrect, or biased
data, it will make bad decisions
2.
The Engine: What is Machine Learning?
In traditional computer programming, a human writes strict rules.
For example: "If an email
contains the word 'Winner', move it to the Spam folder."
Machine Learning (ML) changes this.
Instead of writing rules, we give the computer data and let
it figure out the rules by itself.
● The Analogy: Imagine teaching a child to recognize a dog.
You don’t give them a manual
of rules about ear size and tail length.
You show them 50 dogs and say, "This is a dog."
Eventually, the child's brain recognizes the pattern of a dog.
Machine Learning does the
exact same thing with data.
3.
The Three Ways AI Learns
Scientists train AI using three primary methods.
A.
Supervised Learning (Learning with a Teacher)
This is the most common type of AI training.
We give the AI data where the answer is already
provided.
These answers are called labels.
● Example: We show the AI 10,000 photos of houses, and each photo is labeled with its
actual selling price.
The AI studies the photos and learns how size, location, and
bedrooms affect the price.
Now, when you show it a new photo of a house, it can guess
the price accurately.
B.
Unsupervised Learning (Learning Alone)
Here, we give the AI data with no labels and no answers.
We ask the AI to find hidden patterns
on its own.
● Example: A streaming service gives an AI a list of millions of users and the songs they
like.
The AI automatically groups users with similar tastes together into "clusters,"
allowing the system to recommend new music.
C.
Reinforcement Learning (Trial and Error)
This method uses a system of rewards and penalties.
The AI is placed in an environment and
learns by trying things out.
● Example: To teach an AI to play a video game, it gets "points" (rewards) for staying alive
and penalties for crashing.
After playing millions of times, it learns the perfect strategy to
win.
4.
The Brain: Deep Learning & Neural Networks
You have likely heard the term Deep Learning.
This is just a highly advanced type of Machine
Learning.
Deep Learning uses Artificial Neural Networks, which are software systems loosely inspired by
the human brain.
● Think of a neural network as a giant assembly line of digital filters.
● When you upload a photo of a face, the first layer of the network detects basic lines and
edges.
● The next layer combines those lines to recognize shapes like eyes and noses.
● The final layer puts it all together to say, "That is a human face."
Deep Learning is the technology behind self-driving cars, facial recognition, and smart tools like
ChatGPT.

modules.title: Module 3: Generative AI and the Future of Work
modules.text:
Module 3: Generative AI and the Future of Work
We learned how Machine Learning looks at data to recognize patterns.
Now, we are exploring
Generative AI—the technology that uses those patterns to create brand new content.
Instead of just analyzing data, Generative AI creates things: text, images, music, and even
computer code.
1.
What is Generative AI?
Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that generates new content based on user
prompts.
It is powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).
These models have read billions of pages of
human text from books, articles, and websites.
Because they have seen so much human
language, they understand how words fit together.
● The Predictor Analogy: Think of an LLM as a highly advanced version of the
autocomplete feature on your smartphone.
When you type a prompt, the AI predicts the
next most logical word, sentence, and paragraph based on all the text it has ever read.
2.
Text vs.
Image Generators
Generative AI primarily fits into two popular categories:
A.
Text Generators (The Writers)
Tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude can write, summarize, and brainstorm.
● How they help: They can draft emails, translate languages, write essays, code software,
or summarize a 50-page report into three bullet points.
B.
Image Generators (The Artists)
Tools like Midjourney, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion create visuals from scratch.
● How they help: Instead of searching stock photo websites, a designer can type "a
cinematic photo of an astronaut riding a horse on Mars," and the AI will generate that
exact image in seconds.
3.
The Art of the Prompt
The quality of AI output depends entirely on your instruction.
This instruction is called a prompt.
The emerging skill of writing great prompts is called Prompt Engineering.
To get the best results from a text AI, use the C-T-C Framework:
● Context: Tell the AI who it is.
(e.g., "You are a professional social media manager.")
● Task: Clearly state what you need.
(e.g., "Write three Instagram captions about our new
eco-friendly water bottle.")
● Constraints: Give it boundaries.
(e.g., "Keep each caption under 50 words and use an
energetic tone.")
4.
The Critical Catch: Hallucinations
Generative AI is brilliant, but it has a major flaw: Hallucinations.
Because these systems predict words based on mathematical patterns rather than looking up
verified facts, they can confidently make things up.
● An AI might invent a fake historical date, quote a law that does not exist, or generate a
broken math formula.
● The Golden Rule of Generative AI: Always fact-check the output.
Treat the AI like a
brilliant but slightly careless intern.
5.
AI and the Future of Work
AI is not taking over the world, but it is changing how we work.
● The Shift: AI is shifting humans from creators to editors.
Instead of spending three hours
writing a generic business proposal from scratch, a human uses AI to draft it in ten
seconds, then spends twenty minutes polishing, refining, and humanizing it.
● The Reality: AI likely won't replace your job, but a professional who knows how to use AI
might replace someone who doesn't.

bullets.text: Generative AI is a type of artificial intelligence that generates new content based on user prompts.
It is powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).
These models have read billions of pages of human text from books, articles, and websites.
Because they have seen so much human language, they understand how words fit together.
The Predictor Analogy: Think of an LLM as a highly advanced version of the autocomplete feature on your smartphone.
When you type a prompt, the AI predicts the next most logical word, sentence, and paragraph based on all the text it has ever read.
Generative AI primarily fits into two popular categories: Text Generators (The Writers) and Image Generators (The Artists).
Tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude can write, summarize, and brainstorm.
They can draft emails, translate languages, write essays, code software, or summarize a 50-page report into three bullet points.
Tools like Midjourney, DALL-E, and Stable Diffusion create visuals from scratch.
Instead of searching stock photo websites, a designer can type 'a cinematic photo of an astronaut riding a horse on
The quality of AI output depends entirely on your instruction.
This instruction is called a prompt.
The emerging skill of writing great prompts is called Prompt Engineering.
To get the best results from a text AI, use the C-T-C Framework:
Context: Tell the AI who it is. (e.g., 'You are a professional social media manager.')
Task: Clearly state what you need. (e.g., 'Write three Instagram captions about our new eco-friendly water bottle.')
Constraints: Give it boundaries. (e.g., 'Keep each caption under 50 words and use an energetic tone.')
Generative AI is brilliant, but it has a major flaw: Hallucinations.
Because these systems predict words based on mathematical patterns rather than looking up verified facts, they can confidently make things up.
An AI might invent a fake historical date, quote a law that does not exist, or generate a broken math formula.
The Golden Rule of Generative AI: Always fact-check the output.
Treat the AI like a brilliant but slightly careless intern.
AI is not taking over the world, but it is changing how we work.
The Shift: AI is shifting humans from creators to editors.

The Reality: AI likely won't replace your job, but a professional who knows how to use AI might replace someone who doesn't.

modules.title: Module 4: AI in the Real World
modules.text:
Module 4: AI in the Real World
Now that you know what AI is and how it generates content, let’s look at how it impacts our
everyday lives.
AI is no longer a technology of the future; it is actively running behind the scenes
of our favorite apps, industries, and services.
1.
AI in Entertainment and Media
You likely interact with AI daily without even realizing it through recommendation systems.
● Streaming Services: Platforms like Netflix, Spotify, and YouTube use unsupervised
machine learning.
They track your watch history, skip rates, and search habits to predict
exactly what show or song will keep you hooked.
● Social Media: Feeds on Instagram, TikTok, and X use AI to analyze how many seconds
you linger on a post.
The algorithm then automatically curates a personalized timeline
tailored to your psychology.
2.
AI in Healthcare
AI is revolutionizing medicine by assisting doctors and saving lives.
● Disease Detection: Deep learning algorithms can scan thousands of X-rays, MRIs, and
CT scans.
They often detect tiny tumors or fractures faster and more accurately than
human eyes.
● Drug Discovery: Developing a new medicine usually takes scientists over a decade.
AI
can simulate millions of chemical combinations in seconds, shortening the drug
discovery timeline to just a few months.
3.
AI in Finance and Shopping
Money and commerce rely heavily on automated algorithms.
● Fraud Prevention: When you swipe your credit card, an AI instantly checks if the
transaction matches your usual spending habits.
If you live in New York and your card is
suddenly swiped in Paris, the AI flags it as fraud immediately.
● E-Commerce: Websites like Amazon use AI to forecast inventory demands and change
prices in real-time based on supply, demand, and your personal browsing history.
4.
AI in Transport and Travel
Moving from point A to point B is increasingly managed by smart software.
● Navigation Apps: Google Maps and Apple Maps use AI to analyze historical traffic
patterns, live user speeds, and construction data to calculate your fastest route.
● Autopilot & Autonomous Driving: Commercial airplanes fly on AI autopilot for most of
their journey.
Meanwhile, self-driving cars use cameras and radar to process road
environments instantly.

modules.title: Module 5: The Darkside of AI (Ethics, Bias, Safety)
modules.text:
Module 5: The Darkside of AI (Ethics, Bias, Safety)
While AI offers incredible benefits, it also brings massive challenges.
Because AI is built by
humans and trained on human data, it inherits our flaws, mistakes, and prejudices.
1.
The Problem with Algorithmic Bias
Remember the golden rule from Module 2: Garbage in, garbage out.
If an AI is trained on
biased data, its decisions will be biased.
● Real-World Example: A major tech company built an AI hiring tool to sort through job
resumes.
Because the historical data showed that most past software engineers were
men, the AI mistakenly learned that men were preferable candidates and actively
downgraded resumes containing the word "women's" (e.g., "women's chess club").
2.
Deepfakes and Misinformation
Generative AI makes it incredibly easy to alter reality.
● Deepfakes: These are AI-generated videos, images, or audio clips that look and sound
exactly like real people saying or doing things they never did.
● The Danger: Deepfakes can be used to scam individuals, manipulate political elections,
or ruin reputations by spreading highly convincing fake news.
3.
Copyright and Intellectual Property
Where do AI models get their knowledge?
They scrape billions of images and articles from the
open internet.
● The Controversy: Many human artists, authors, and journalists are suing AI companies.
They argue that AI models are using their copyrighted work without permission,
payment, or credit to generate competing content.
4.
Workforce Displacement
AI will automate many repetitive tasks currently done by humans.
● The Shift: Jobs involving basic data entry, simple customer service, basic copywriting,
and routine coding are experiencing major shifts.
While AI creates new tech jobs, it
requires workers to quickly upskill to avoid being left behind.

modules.title: Module 6: Master the Machine (Prompting basics)
modules.text:
Module 6: Master the Machine (Prompting basics)
To close out this course, you will learn the most critical practical skill for the AI era: Prompt
Engineering.
This section teaches you exactly how to talk to an AI to get perfect results on your
very first try.
1.
Avoid the "Google Search" Mistake
Most beginners treat AI like a search engine, typing short keywords like: "marketing plan for
coffee shop."
● The Result: The AI gives a generic, boring response because it has no context.
● The Fix: Treat the AI like a highly capable human assistant.
Give it specific rules,
background information, and a clear goal.
2.
The Golden Prompt Blueprint
Whenever you want an AI to write, brainstorm, or analyze, use this four-part formula:
\(\text{Role}+\text{Context}+\text{Task}+\text{Format}\)
● Role: Tell the AI who it is.
(e.g., "Act as a fitness coach.")
● Context: Give it the background story.
(e.g., "I am a busy office worker who wants to lose
5kg, but I only have 20 minutes a day to exercise.")
● Task: Clearly state what you need done.
(e.g., "Create a 5-day home workout plan.")
● Format: Tell it how to present the answer.
(e.g., "Put this in a clean markdown table with
columns for exercise name, reps, and rest time.")
3.
Three Pro-Tips for Better AI Results
● Give Examples (Few-Shot Prompting): If you want the AI to write a specific style of
newsletter, paste two of your past newsletters first and say, "Learn my style from these
examples, then write a new post about..."
● Iterate and Refine: Never settle for the first answer.
If the response is too long, tell the AI:
"Make it 30% shorter and more casual."
● Ask the AI to Ask You Questions: If you aren't sure what details to provide, type: "I want
to launch a website.
Ask me 5 questions one by one to gather the info you need to build
a strategy."
